chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Jameel ibn Salih, from Hisham ibn Ahmad, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shazaan, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, all together, from Salima, the slave-girl of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I was in the presence of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when death presented itself to him, so he fell unconscious. When he regained consciousness, he said: 'Give seventy dinars to al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn, and he was al-Aftas, and give so-and-so such and such, and to so-and-so such and such.' I said: 'Do you want to give a man who attacked you with a blade?' He said: 'Woe be unto you! Do you not read the Quran?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Have you not heard the Word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: Those who join what Allah has bidden to be joined, and have awe of their Lord, and they are fearing the evil Reckoning?'

Ibn Mahboub said in his hadith: 'He attacked you with a blade, intending to kill you?' So he said: 'Do you want that I should happen to be from those about whom Allah, Blessed and High, said: Those who join what Allah has bidden to be joined, and have awe of their Lord, and they are fearing the evil Reckoning?' Yes, O Salima! Indeed, Allah created Paradise and made it fragrant, and made its aroma fragrant, and its aroma can be found from a travel distance of two thousand years, and it would not be smelt by one disobedient to his parents (Aaq) and one who cuts off relationships.

key_terms.الْأَفْطَسُ: A nickname meaning 'the one with the wide forehead' or 'broad-faced', used here for al-Hasan ibn Ali.
key_terms.بِالشَّفْرَةِ: With the blade (of a sword or dagger), indicating a physical attack.
key_terms.عَاقٌّ: One who is disobedient to his parents.
key_terms.قَاطِعُ رَحِمٍ: One who cuts off family ties/kinship.
key_terms.يَصِلُونَ ما أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ أَنْ يُ: Those who join what Allah has bidden to be joined, referring to maintaining family and social ties.

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam al-Sadiq give money to the man who attacked him with a blade?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (as) demonstrates the virtue of *sabr* and generosity by bequeathing wealth to his assassins, specifically citing Quran 13:21 to justify maintaining ties (*silat al-rahim*) with those who wronged him. He contrasts this with the spiritual consequence of cutting kinship, noting that the disbeliever or one who severs family ties will not perceive the fragrance of Paradise, which extends for a thousand years' journey. This highlights the Shia emphasis on forgiving enemies as a means of securing divine reward and preserving familial bonds even in death.
